fitSummary.roleFocus: Senior backend engineer for product teams shipping in real-world constraints
fitSummary.collaborationStyle: Works directly with product, design, and data stakeholders to scope risk-first delivery
fitSummary.timezoneOverlap: EU hours with consistent overlap for UK and US East Coast
fitSummary.availability: Open to full-time and long-term product roles

interviewPolicy.statement: I do not run trivia-based screening. I prefer real system discussion, evidence review, and tradeoff analysis.
interviewPolicy.prompt: If you want to assess me, use the artifacts below and ask how decisions were made under constraints.

seniorSignals.title: Reliability
seniorSignals.claim: I treat incidents as both response and design feedback loops.

seniorSignals.title: Performance
seniorSignals.claim: I profile bottlenecks before rewriting and optimize the highest-cost path first.

seniorSignals.title: Architecture
seniorSignals.claim: I choose service boundaries based on ownership and failure isolation, not fashion.

seniorSignals.title: Data
seniorSignals.claim: I run risky data migrations with reversible steps and production safety gates.

seniorSignals.title: Delivery
seniorSignals.claim: I ship meaningful increments while negotiating scope and timeline constraints.

seniorSignals.title: Quality
seniorSignals.claim: I design testing strategy around business risk and failure modes, not checklist coverage.

seniorSignals.title: Stakeholder Management
seniorSignals.claim: I keep delivery predictable by making decision tradeoffs explicit to non-engineering partners.

seniorSignals.title: Operations
seniorSignals.claim: I use lightweight runbooks and ownership clarity to reduce repeat production failures.

seniorSignals.title: Consistency
seniorSignals.claim: I choose delivery guarantees explicitly and build compensating mechanisms where strict consistency is too costly.

seniorSignals.title: Planning
seniorSignals.claim: I can reset failing delivery plans by narrowing scope and adding explicit risk checkpoints.

caseStudies.title: Checkout API latency and timeout recovery
caseStudies.context: Core checkout endpoint became unstable after demand spikes and regional traffic growth.
caseStudies.situation: P95 latency drifted above user tolerance during peak windows, causing timeout-related drop-off in checkout completion.
constraints: Shared database with legacy reporting workloads
Limited ability to add new infrastructure immediately
options: Rewrite checkout service end-to-end
Horizontal scale only and accept cost increase
Profile hot paths, isolate expensive query patterns, and stage targeted fixes
caseStudies.decision: Chose targeted performance work: query plan fixes, request shaping, and idempotent retry handling at failure boundaries.
tradeoffs: Did not remove all legacy coupling in phase one
Needed additional operational guardrails while rollout stabilized
caseStudies.outcome: Reduced checkout timeout rate and restored predictable peak behavior while roadmap delivery continued. Exact KPI values are confidential but were reviewed with leadership post-release.
learnings: Profiling before refactoring avoids expensive false starts
Latency and reliability should be treated as one system
discussionPrompts: How would you prioritize fixes if the bottleneck shifts every week?
Which latency regressions can be accepted temporarily and why?
evaluationSignals: Explains baseline and bottleneck identification before solutioning
Discusses cost, risk, and rollback while improving performance
antiPatterns: Treating retries as reliability without idempotency guarantees

caseStudies.title: Subscription domain boundary split in a live system
caseStudies.context: Monolithic subscription and billing logic slowed delivery and raised incident blast radius.
caseStudies.situation: A single service owned subscription lifecycle, invoicing logic, and partner sync integrations, creating cross-team contention.
constraints: Contract commitments tied to billing correctness
Mixed seniority engineering team and active feature pressure
options: Big-bang migration to new services
Keep monolith and patch local pain points
Incremental boundary split with compatibility layer and progressive ownership transfer
caseStudies.decision: Used incremental extraction with explicit ownership boundaries and staged read/write migration controls.
tradeoffs: Temporary duplication of logic while traffic shifted
Longer transition period to protect billing correctness
caseStudies.outcome: Delivery coordination improved across teams, incident impact scope narrowed, and new feature lead time decreased after boundary stabilization.
learnings: Boundary decisions must map to team ownership, not only technical purity
Migration safety wins over implementation speed when financial correctness is involved
discussionPrompts: When does incremental extraction become too slow to justify?
How do you keep product delivery moving during domain migration?
evaluationSignals: Can articulate ownership boundaries and coupling costs
Can explain staged rollout and fallback strategy
antiPatterns: Service split based only on technical layers

caseStudies.title: Incident storm containment without roadmap freeze
caseStudies.context: A burst of production incidents consumed delivery capacity and created stakeholder distrust.
caseStudies.situation: Multiple unrelated failures appeared across API, queue processing, and reporting paths over two release cycles.
constraints: No room for hiring or major platform migration
On-call fatigue and limited senior bandwidth
options: Pause all feature work until incidents disappear
Continue roadmap as planned and address incidents ad-hoc
Split roadmap into reliability-critical and business-critical lanes with explicit acceptance gates
caseStudies.decision: Introduced a two-lane delivery plan with reliability gates, weekly failure class review, and a short incident-prevention backlog.
tradeoffs: Some non-critical features were delayed
Team had to adopt stricter definition-of-done criteria
caseStudies.outcome: Incident frequency dropped over the following release window while core commitments continued, restoring delivery predictability.
learnings: Reliability work must be planned as delivery work, not side work
Explicit gate criteria reduce conflict during prioritization
discussionPrompts: How would you negotiate reliability work with sales pressure?
Which incidents justify immediate roadmap interruption?
evaluationSignals: Shows prioritization model under competing constraints
Connects reliability investment to business outcomes
antiPatterns: Declaring reliability priority without scope changes

caseStudies.title: Release train stabilization in a multi-team backend
caseStudies.context: Frequent release slips came from late integration failures and unclear dependency ownership.
caseStudies.situation: Three teams shipped into the same release train with hidden coupling discovered only in final validation.
constraints: Quarterly release commitments to enterprise clients
Mixed maturity in engineering planning practices
No budget for heavy new tooling
options: Introduce a heavyweight release board process
Keep current process and absorb delays
Adopt lightweight dependency mapping and pre-integration checkpoints
caseStudies.decision: Implemented dependency declarations, cutline ownership, and pre-integration checks one sprint earlier.
tradeoffs: Slightly higher upfront planning overhead
Required product owners to make earlier tradeoff calls
caseStudies.outcome: Reduced late-stage surprises and improved release confidence, with fewer last-week rollbacks.
learnings: Delivery failure often starts at planning interfaces, not implementation
Earlier integration checkpoints lower end-stage stress
discussionPrompts: How early should cross-team dependency risk be surfaced?
What should be the minimum release-readiness evidence?
evaluationSignals: Makes dependency risk visible before coding completes
Balances process overhead with practical release outcomes
antiPatterns: Relying on heroics in release week

decisionRecords.title: Boundary choice: orders vs payments
decisionRecords.context: Order and payment operations were tightly coupled, causing coordinated releases for unrelated changes.
decisionRecords.situation: Shared models and release pipelines increased cross-team dependency and delayed ownership.
constraints: Need to preserve existing integration contracts
options: Keep one service with modular code
Split by technical layer
Split by domain ownership with explicit API contracts
decisionRecords.decision: Separated orders and payments by business ownership with contract tests and strict dependency direction.
tradeoffs: Initial integration overhead
Required stronger API governance discipline
decisionRecords.outcome: Reduced release coupling and clearer incident ownership between domains.
learnings: Ownership boundaries should drive architecture decisions
Contract clarity matters more than internal elegance
discussionPrompts: How do you choose boundaries when team ownership is unstable?
What contracts are mandatory before extraction?
evaluationSignals: Ties architecture to organization and failure isolation
Can explain coupling costs in delivery terms
antiPatterns: Ignoring ownership model in boundary design

decisionRecords.title: Migration strategy: phased writes before reads
decisionRecords.context: Critical dataset required schema evolution without downtime.
decisionRecords.situation: Legacy consumers depended on old schema assumptions while product roadmap required new structure.
options: Big-bang schema switch
Dual-read + dual-write from day one
Expand-contract with phased write/read cutover
decisionRecords.decision: Applied expand-contract pattern with validation checkpoints and rollback toggles per stage.
tradeoffs: Longer migration timeline
Temporary storage and logic duplication
decisionRecords.outcome: Schema transitioned safely with controlled risk and no customer-visible outage.
learnings: Migration confidence comes from reversible steps
Operational rehearsals are part of engineering work
discussionPrompts: How do you prove a migration is safe before final cutover?
When should you abandon a migration strategy mid-flight?
evaluationSignals: Defines rollback at each phase
Discusses data correctness checks beyond happy path
antiPatterns: Coupling schema cutover to one deploy

decisionRecords.title: Observability approach: detection tied to action
decisionRecords.context: High alert volume created fatigue, while critical regressions were still missed.
decisionRecords.situation: Monitoring existed but lacked runbook mapping and clear ownership for response.
constraints: No appetite for expensive tooling overhaul
options: Increase alerts for every known failure mode
Suppress alerts and rely on manual checks
Prioritize actionable alerting with runbook links and ownership tags
decisionRecords.decision: Implemented severity-based alerting with incident runbook linkage and post-incident prevention checkpoints.
tradeoffs: Initial tuning period with false positives
Required process consistency from engineering and product
decisionRecords.outcome: Faster incident triage and fewer repeat production issues from the same classes of failure.
learnings: Visibility without response design is noise
Incident reviews should produce concrete prevention actions
discussionPrompts: Which alerts should page someone at 3am and why?
How do you keep runbooks from becoming stale artifacts?
evaluationSignals: Can connect metrics to operational decisions
Can define ownership and escalation paths clearly
antiPatterns: More alerts as the default reliability strategy
No feedback loop from incident review to backlog

decisionRecords.title: Cache strategy: freshness budget over blanket caching
decisionRecords.context: Read pressure increased infrastructure cost and occasional stale data complaints.
decisionRecords.situation: Teams wanted aggressive caching, but data freshness requirements varied heavily by workflow.
constraints: Limited team time for complex invalidation logic
options: Cache everything with long TTL
No cache and absorb database cost
Define freshness budgets per workflow and choose cache strategy accordingly
decisionRecords.decision: Introduced freshness tiers with explicit TTL and invalidation strategy per endpoint category.
tradeoffs: More upfront design discussion
Needed endpoint-level observability for hit ratio and staleness
decisionRecords.outcome: Reduced read load and cost while preserving correctness in freshness-sensitive paths.
learnings: Caching is a product decision as much as an infrastructure decision
Freshness expectations should be explicit in API design
discussionPrompts: Where would you avoid caching even under heavy load?
How do you monitor cache correctness, not only cache hit ratio?
evaluationSignals: Recognizes different consistency needs per workflow
Understands invalidation and stale data risk
antiPatterns: Using cache as a substitute for bad query design

decisionRecords.title: Testing strategy: risk map before framework choice
decisionRecords.context: Team debates focused on test tooling, while high-risk flows remained under-tested.
decisionRecords.situation: Coverage increased but production failures still came from integration boundaries and migration paths.
constraints: Need to keep developer feedback fast
options: Target high global coverage percentages
Rely primarily on manual QA
Map failure risk by workflow and align test depth by risk
decisionRecords.decision: Set risk tiers and used focused integration tests for critical paths, lighter coverage for low-risk flows.
tradeoffs: Requires periodic risk-map updates
Some low-risk regressions may still slip
decisionRecords.outcome: Improved signal from test failures and reduced escaped defects in high-impact workflows.
learnings: Coverage is an input, not a product quality guarantee
Testing strategy should evolve with system risk profile
discussionPrompts: How do you explain risk-based testing to non-technical stakeholders?
When do you promote a workflow from low-risk to high-risk testing?
evaluationSignals: Can reason about risk rather than tool preference
Balances confidence with execution speed

decisionRecords.title: Background processing model: at-least-once with compensations
decisionRecords.context: Business workflow required asynchronous processing across external systems with intermittent failure.
decisionRecords.situation: Team initially expected exactly-once behavior from queue delivery and hit duplicate side effects.
constraints: External providers with limited reliability guarantees
options: Attempt strict exactly-once transport
Disable retries and accept data loss risk
Adopt at-least-once handling with idempotent consumers and compensating actions
decisionRecords.decision: Standardized at-least-once processing with explicit deduplication and reconciliation jobs.
tradeoffs: Additional complexity in state tracking
Requires clear ownership for compensation workflows
decisionRecords.outcome: Processing became more predictable under partial failures, with fewer unresolved data mismatches.
learnings: Consistency guarantees must be explicit in architecture docs
Compensation flows are product behavior, not just technical plumbing
discussionPrompts: Where would you use compensation over strict transactional guarantees?
How do you surface reconciliation debt to product owners?
evaluationSignals: Understands delivery guarantees and failure semantics
Connects processing model to business correctness

productionPatterns.title: Idempotency with bounded retries
productionPatterns.context: External dependency instability caused duplicate operations during retry storms.
productionPatterns.situation: Network and timeout errors triggered retries that sometimes repeated non-safe operations.
constraints: Business flow requires exactly-once side effects
options: Disable retries
Keep naive retries and handle duplicate cleanup manually
Apply idempotency keys, dedupe store, and bounded retry policy
productionPatterns.decision: Standardized idempotency key handling on write paths with bounded exponential retries and dead-letter escalation.
tradeoffs: Extra storage and key lifecycle management
Slight latency increase on guarded operations
productionPatterns.outcome: Reduced duplicate side effects and improved recovery behavior under transient failures.
learnings: Retries without idempotency create hidden reliability debt
Failure-path design is first-class architecture
discussionPrompts: Which operations need idempotency keys first?
How do you manage key retention policy?
evaluationSignals: Understands idempotency boundary and state model
Discusses retry policy with dead-letter handling
antiPatterns: Idempotency implemented only at transport layer
productionPatterns.snippet: receive request -> check idempotency key -> if seen return prior result -> execute operation -> persist result -> ack

productionPatterns.title: Database migration safety rollout
productionPatterns.context: Business-critical table needed schema and indexing changes under active traffic.
productionPatterns.situation: Direct schema changes risked lock contention and prolonged degraded performance.
options: Single transaction migration
Pause writes during migration
Expand-contract with background backfill and staged cutover
productionPatterns.decision: Executed phased migration: additive schema, background backfill, validation checks, and controlled cutover.
tradeoffs: Longer operational window
Need to maintain dual compatibility temporarily
productionPatterns.outcome: Delivered schema evolution without downtime and with measurable rollback safety at each phase.
learnings: Migration sequencing is operational engineering
Safety checkpoints prevent irreversible mistakes
discussionPrompts: What makes a migration phase reversible?
How do you monitor backfill safety under live traffic?
evaluationSignals: Defines checkpoints and rollback criteria
Discusses lock behavior and traffic safety
productionPatterns.snippet: phase 1 add nullable columns -> phase 2 dual write -> phase 3 backfill + verify -> phase 4 switch reads -> phase 5 remove legacy fields

productionPatterns.title: Incident playbook with prevention loop
productionPatterns.context: Incident response quality varied by who was online, creating inconsistent outcomes.
productionPatterns.situation: Teams had tribal knowledge but no lightweight shared playbook for escalation and recovery.
constraints: Need to keep documentation overhead low
options: Full formal incident management rollout
Ad-hoc response only
Lightweight severity playbook with explicit ownership and post-incident actions
productionPatterns.decision: Adopted simple severity matrix, communication template, and mandatory follow-up action tracking for recurring failure classes.
tradeoffs: Requires team discipline to keep runbook current
Some edge cases still need live judgment
productionPatterns.outcome: Improved consistency in incident handling and reduced recurrence of known failure modes.
learnings: Good incident process optimizes decision quality under stress
The value is in repeatable response, not process theater
discussionPrompts: How do you keep communication useful under pressure?
Which post-incident actions deserve immediate prioritization?
evaluationSignals: Can run incident flow with clear ownership
Connects incident outcomes to prevention backlog
productionPatterns.snippet: detect -> triage severity -> assign incident owner -> stabilize service -> communicate status -> run post-incident review -> track prevention task

productionPatterns.title: Outbox + inbox for cross-service consistency
productionPatterns.context: Domain events were occasionally lost between write and publish, causing downstream state drift.
productionPatterns.situation: Direct publish after transaction commit created race conditions during transient failures.
options: Best-effort publish without persistence
Synchronous cross-service call chain
Persist outbox in same transaction and consume with deduplicated inbox
productionPatterns.decision: Implemented transactional outbox on producer side and inbox deduplication on consumer side.
tradeoffs: More storage and operational complexity
Eventual consistency requires stakeholder alignment
productionPatterns.outcome: Reduced lost updates and gave teams a reliable reconciliation path for cross-service messaging.
learnings: Event guarantees must be explicit, not assumed
Reconciliation tools are part of production readiness
discussionPrompts: When does eventual consistency become unacceptable?
How do you expose reconciliation state to operators?
evaluationSignals: Explains producer and consumer guarantees clearly
Understands replay, dedupe, and ordering tradeoffs
antiPatterns: Assuming broker durability solves producer atomicity
productionPatterns.snippet: db tx: write business row + outbox row -> outbox worker publishes -> consumer inbox dedupe -> apply handler

productionPatterns.title: Circuit breaker with controlled degradation
productionPatterns.context: Dependency outages cascaded into full API failure for non-critical operations.
productionPatterns.situation: Synchronous calls to unstable downstreams blocked threads and exhausted resources.
constraints: Must keep core user path available
options: Keep retrying until downstream recovers
Fail all dependent requests immediately
Use circuit breaker thresholds with fallback responses for non-critical paths
productionPatterns.decision: Added failure thresholds and fallback behavior for non-critical dependency calls, preserving critical workflows.
tradeoffs: Users may see reduced functionality during outage
Needs clear monitoring to avoid stuck-open circuits
productionPatterns.outcome: Prevented cascading failures and preserved core path availability during partner downtime.
learnings: Graceful degradation is a product decision
Circuit policies need continuous tuning
discussionPrompts: Which flows deserve fallback versus hard fail?
How do you detect circuit misconfiguration in production?
evaluationSignals: Can define failure thresholds and fallback scope
Understands tradeoff between availability and feature completeness
antiPatterns: Fallbacks that hide critical data loss
productionPatterns.snippet: if downstream failure rate > threshold -> open circuit -> return fallback -> half-open probe -> close on healthy responses

productionPatterns.title: SLO burn-rate alerting for incident triage
productionPatterns.context: Teams lacked a shared threshold for deciding when reliability degradation was truly urgent.
productionPatterns.situation: Alert noise was high and severity decisions were inconsistent between responders.
options: Alert on every threshold breach
Use only static latency alarms
Alert on burn-rate against error budgets over short and long windows
productionPatterns.decision: Adopted multi-window burn-rate alerts tied to severity levels and escalation policy.
tradeoffs: Requires reliable SLI definitions
Needs team education on error-budget concepts
productionPatterns.outcome: Improved triage consistency and reduced unnecessary high-severity paging.
learnings: Alert quality matters more than alert quantity
Shared severity language reduces response friction
discussionPrompts: How would you define SLIs for mixed workloads?
What burn-rate thresholds are practical for small teams?
evaluationSignals: Understands relationship between SLOs and incident urgency
Can operationalize thresholds into response policy
productionPatterns.snippet: window short burn-rate > X and window long burn-rate > Y -> page; else ticket and review

redFlags: Scope expansion without owner-level tradeoff decisions
Coverage metrics used as a proxy for product risk reduction
Interview processes that optimize for definitions over decision quality
Platform rewrites proposed before baseline bottlenecks are measured
